The man behind Chandler: Netflix documentary explores his life, struggles and legacy

Directed by Emmy Award winner Mary Robertson, the series will premiere globally on Netflix on October 27.

Maryam Hassan

02 September, 2026 01:56 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Reuters/Fred Prouser/File Photo

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: Netflix is making a three-part documentary series about the life and legacy of Friends star Matthew Perry, exploring the actor’s journey beyond his most famous character, Chandler Bing. The documentary will revisit Perry’s rise to global fame, his struggles with addiction and recovery, and the personal life behind the actor millions of viewers grew up watching on television.

The documentary series is titled The One About Matthew Perry  and is directed and produced by Emmy Award winner Mary Robertson. The three-part series is set to premiere globally on Netflix on October 27, 2026. It will feature interviews with people who knew Perry closely, including his younger sister Mia Perry Bowick. His family has also opened their private archives for the project.

“Matthew Perry was one of the comedic geniuses of our time. Through his many film, TV, and stage performances, and his unforgettable portrayal of Chandler, he made millions of us laugh,” Robertson said.

Show Full Article

Perry became a household name after his role as Chandler Bing in Friends . The sitcom premiered in 1994 and went on to become one of television’s biggest shows, with Perry’s comic timing making Chandler one of its most recognisable characters. He starred alongside Jennifer Aniston, Courteney Cox, Lisa Kudrow, Matt LeBlanc and David Schwimmer.

Also Read: Year after Matthew Perry’s death, spotlight on ‘Ketamine Queen’ Jasveen Sangha, set to stand trial in 2025

A life beyond Chandler Bing However, his life away from the screen was much more complicated. Perry struggled with addiction for years and went through several attempts at recovery. He later became increasingly open about his experiences, using his public platform to speak about addiction and help others dealing with similar struggles.

In 2022, Perry published his memoir, Friends, Lovers, and the Big Terrible Thing , in which he wrote about his childhood, acting career, relationships, and battle with addiction. His experiences with substance abuse affected his work and personal life, making his public discussions about recovery an important part of his later years.

Perry died on October 28, 2023, at the age of 54. He was found unresponsive at his home in Los Angeles. According to the Los Angeles County medical examiner, the acute effects of an anesthetic , ketamine, contributed to his death, with drowning, coronary artery disease, and the effects of buprenorphine also listed as contributing factors.

His death was followed by a criminal investigation into how he obtained ketamine. Several people, including doctors and an associate who worked with Perry, were charged in connection with his death.

However, Netflix’s documentary is not primarily about how Matthew Perry died. Instead, it looks at the life he lived before his death – from becoming one of television’s biggest comedy stars to publicly confronting addiction and trying to turn his experiences into something that could help others.

Edited by Maryam Hassan

Over half of Americans polled say they are spending too much time on their phones, Pew finds

Almost half of US adults attempted to reduce their smartphone use over the past year, but only a quarter said they were extremely successful.

Himanshi Aggarwal

02 September, 2026 12:32 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Kiyoshi Ota/Bloomberg

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: Between scrolling, notifications, and messages, smartphones are becoming increasingly ingrained in the daily routine. A new survey by the Pew Research Center found that over half of the adults in the United States believe they spend “too much” time on their phones.

The survey conducted between May and June 2026 found that 53% of adults find their phone screen time   excessive, about a third find it adequate, and only 3% say that they spend too little time on the device. These findings are based on a survey of 9,750 U.S. adults.

“Younger adults stand out for describing their smartphone use as excessive,” the survey noted.

Show Full Article

Younger adults struggle most to cut back Seven in ten adults under the age of 30 noted that they spend too much time on their phones, and nearly as many in their 30s and 40s felt the same way. The perception of phone overuse declines with age, with about half of those in their 50s and early 60s saying they use their phones too much, compared with just a quarter of adults aged 65 and above.

Many people are trying to push back. Nearly half (45%) of the adults surveyed say they have attempted to cut back on their phone time in the past year. Of those who tried, just one in four said they were extremely successful, while 52% considered themselves somewhat successful and 23% said they were not too or not at all successful. Younger adults were far more likely than older ones to have made the attempt.

Even so, phones remain a constant presence. About a quarter of adults say they use their smartphone almost constantly, and most of the rest check it several times a day.

The pattern is most prevalent among the younger age groups, with more than four in ten adults under 30 report almost constant use, and another 60% say they use them several times a day. Adults under 30 are the most likely to report almost constant use (42%), compared with 9% of those aged 65 and older.

Also Read: Concerts, clubs want people to keep their phones away. It’s a new trend taking over the US

Smartphones help people stay connected, but they may hurt sleep “Americans see both benefits and downsides when asked about the impact that smartphones have on people’s lives,” the survey noted.

The personal reflection on the impact of phone use is varied. Most say smartphones help them stay informed and stay connected with others. Views on productivity and mood are more divided, with many people saying phones neither help nor hurt much.

Adults under 30 are the most likely to say their smartphone hurts their productivity levels.

Sleep is the clearest downside.

“Much larger shares say their smartphones hurt than help the amount of sleep they get (41% vs. 5%), the survey concluded. “Still, nearly half say their phone has no impact on their sleep.”

Edited by Maryam Hassan

By Alasdair Pal and Kanishka Singh SYDNEY/WASHINGTON, Sept 1 (Reuters) – The United States and Australia on Wednesday announced a combined $580 million in funding for the Pacific Islands, as both nations battle China for influence in the region.

Australia will offer a A$600 million ($430 million) package to combat drug smuggling in the region at a meeting of the Pacific Islands Forum in Palau, including funds for enhanced aerial surveillance and more training for police and border officials.

“The Pacific is our home and our family. That’s why it’s in Australia’s interests to work with our Pacific partners to combat organised crime,” Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in a statement.

Show Full Article

“For the good of every country in the region, including our own – we need to work together to stamp out the illicit drug trade.”

In a separate announcement, the U.S. State Department said it will provide $150 million in funding to the region, including $60 million to help Pacific Islands countries address the global energy crisis by expanding fuel storage capacity and supporting grid stability.

Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau announced the funding at the forum that has so far been dominated by a spat over Taiwan’s participation.

China, a major donor to the Pacific that views Taiwan as its own territory, has objected to the democratically run island’s presence at the annual meeting of the 18-member forum.

Members Australia and New Zealand said on Tuesday the bloc would decide the guest list.

Palau, which is hosting this year’s meeting, is among three Pacific nations that have maintained diplomatic ties with Taiwan. The meeting, which began on August 30, will run to September 4.

($1 = 1.4002 Australian dollars)

(Reporting by Alasdair Pal in Sydney and Kanishka Singh in Washington; Editing by Edwina Gibbs)

Massachusetts Democrats renominate Senator Ed Markey in race seen as test on generational change

Reuters

02 September, 2026 07:00 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

By Nolan D. McCaskill WASHINGTON, Sept 1 (Reuters) – U.S. Senator Ed Markey of Massachusetts won renomination on Tuesday, according to U.S. media, as Democratic voters favored the 80-year-old progressive over 47-year-old Seth Moulton, a moderate U.S. representative who ran on generational change.

Markey, who has served in Congress for nearly 50 years, was backed by leading progressives such as Senator Bernie Sanders and U.S. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, as well as most members of the state’s congressional delegation, including U.S. Senator Elizabeth Warren.

No members of the delegation had endorsed Moulton, a moderate U.S. Marine Corps veteran whose supporters included New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill and the Democratic organization VoteVets. The Boston Globe’s editorial board was also behind Moulton, casting him as a necessary agent of change with “proven leadership skills” and positions on key issues that align with most voters.

Show Full Article

Markey had a nearly $2 million fundraising advantage over Moulton and led in recent polls by a double-digit margin. He is heavily favored to win in November. Democrat Kamala Harris carried the state by nearly 25 percentage points in 2024.

Democratic voters across the country this year have often backed younger, more progressive candidates, leading to the ouster of incumbents in primaries in New York, Colorado and Michigan, although in Massachusetts it is the long-serving Senate incumbent who is considered more progressive.

BOSTON HOUSE RACE MIRRORS SENATE CONTEST

A more typical generational challenge is playing out in the Boston area, where moderate U.S. Representative Stephen Lynch, 71, is facing progressive attorney Patrick Roath, 39.

The Boston Globe’s editorial board endorsed Roath, writing that the younger candidate “gives every indication he can do better, think bigger, and aim higher as a member of Congress” than Lynch.

Roath has outraised Lynch, $1.3 million to $910,000, and he has closed in on the incumbent in polling. A survey conducted for Leaders We Deserve, a group that has endorsed Roath, found Lynch’s lead had fallen to seven percentage points. A February poll conducted for Roath showed him trailing Lynch by 26 points. Lynch was reelected in 2024 by a 50-point margin.

Democrats hold all nine Massachusetts House seats and both Senate seats. The winner of the 8th Congressional District primary will be heavily favored to win in November.

(Reporting by Nolan D. McCaskill; Editing by Michael Learmonth, Alistair Bell and Edmund Klamann)
